1. The Real Inventors: Acharya Virasena and Nemicandra
Seven hundred years before the Scottish mathematician John Napier published his work on logarithms in 1614, Indian mathematicians had already systematically laid out the exact principles of logarithmic functions:

Acharya Virasena (8th Century CE): In his monumental commentary Dhavala, the Jain polymath and mathematician Virasena introduced advanced concepts of base-2, base-3, and base-4 logarithms. He called them Ardhaccheda: This translates to "cutting in half" and is mathematically identical to \[\log _{2}x\] (logarithm to the base 2). He explicitly showed that the number of times a number can be divided by 2 matches its ardhaccheda.
Trikaccheda: Logarithm to the base 3 (\[\log _{3}x\]).
Chaturachheda: Logarithm to the base 4 (\[\log _{4}x\]).

2. Acharya Nemicandra (10th Century CE): In his text Trilokasara, Nemicandra advanced this framework. He established operational laws for indices and logarithms, demonstrating that multiplication of numbers corresponds to the addition of their ardhacchedas, and division corresponds to their subtraction. This is the fundamental purpose and core rule of logarithms
